summary: This proposed standard defines the protocol operations of SNMPv2, meaning how its messages are sent and received. It was replaced by RFC 1905.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the SNMPv2 messages themselves: how a manager asks a device for a value, how it reads through a table, how it changes a value and how a device reports something unusual. It also defines the reply codes that say why a request could not be carried out.

questions: difference between snmp trap and inform
subtitle: The messages SNMPv2 sends and receives: how to read values, walk tables, change values and raise notifications.

tldr.problem: A network management station needs to read and change values on devices, and needs to walk through the tables of values those devices hold, without spending one round trip per row.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines seven Protocol Data Units carried inside a message wrapper: GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, SetRequest, Response, InformRequest and SNMPv2-Trap. Every request carries a request-id, an error status and a list of variable bindings.
tldr.outcome: GetNextRequest walks a table one row at a time by asking for the next name in lexicographic order, and GetBulkRequest asks for many rows at once to cut the number of exchanges. The document has been replaced by RFC 1905.

today: RFC 1448 was a Proposed Standard published in April 1993. It has been obsoleted by RFC 1905, which is the current definition of the SNMPv2 protocol operations.

sections.title: What the SNMPv2 Operations Are
sections.content:
A network management system contains several, potentially many, nodes, each with a processing entity termed an agent which has access to management instrumentation; at least one management station; and a management protocol used to convey management information between the agents and the management stations. Operations of the protocol are carried out under an administrative framework which defines both authentication and authorization policies.

Management stations execute management applications which monitor and control network elements. Network elements are devices such as hosts, routers and terminal servers, monitored and controlled through access to their management information.

Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects, residing in a virtual information store termed the Management Information Base (MIB). Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, written using a subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1), termed the Structure of Management Information. The management protocol, version 2 of SNMP, provides for the exchange of messages which convey management information between the agents and the management stations. The form of these messages is a message wrapper which encapsulates a Protocol Data Unit, and the form and meaning of that wrapper is determined by the administrative framework.

The purpose of this document is to define the operations of the protocol with respect to the sending and receiving of the PDUs. The RFC is explicit about one thing it does not do: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMPv2 is the exchange of small messages between a management station and the agents on the devices it looks after. This document defines those messages. Security is handled elsewhere.

sections.title: Roles, Management Information and Access
sections.content:
A SNMPv2 entity may operate in a manager role or an agent role. It acts in an agent role when it performs SNMPv2 management operations in response to received SNMPv2 protocol messages, other than an inform notification, or when it sends trap notifications. It acts in a manager role when it initiates SNMPv2 management operations by generating protocol messages, or when it performs management operations in response to received trap or inform notifications. An entity may support either or both roles, and it can also act as a proxy agent, appearing to be in an agent role but satisfying management requests by acting in a manager role with a remote entity.

The term variable refers to an instance of a non-aggregate object type. A variable binding normally pairs the name of a variable with its associated value, but if an exceptional condition occurs during processing of a retrieval request, a variable binding pairs a name with an indication of that exception. A variable-binding list is a simple list of variable bindings. The name of a variable is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, which is the concatenation of the OBJECT IDENTIFIER of the corresponding object-type with an OBJECT IDENTIFIER fragment identifying the instance.

Three types of access are provided. A request-response interaction, in which a manager sends a request to an agent and the agent responds, is used to retrieve or modify management information associated with the managed device. A second request-response interaction, in which a manager sends a request to another manager and that manager responds, is used to notify a manager of management information associated with another manager. The third type is an unconfirmed interaction, in which an agent sends an unsolicited message, termed a trap, to a manager and no response is returned, used to report an exceptional situation that has resulted in changes to management information.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks and the other answers. A request names a variable and a reply gives its value. A trap is the odd one out: the device sends it unprompted and nobody answers.

sections.title: The PDU Types and Their ASN.1 Form
sections.content:
The protocol defines seven PDU types: GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, Response, SetRequest, InformRequest and SNMPv2-Trap. Each is an ASN.1 choice alternative with its own tag: GetRequest is [0], GetNextRequest is [1], Response is [2], SetRequest is [3], GetBulkRequest is [5], InformRequest is [6] and SNMPv2-Trap is [7]. The tag [4] is obsolete.

Most of the PDUs share a common structure: a request-id of type Integer32, an error-status field that is sometimes ignored, an error-index field of type INTEGER (0..max-bindings), and a variable-bindings field holding a VarBindList. The error-status values run from noError(0) through inconsistentName(18), and include tooBig, noSuchName, badValue, readOnly, genErr, noAccess, wrongType, wrongLength, wrongEncoding, wrongValue, noCreation, inconsistentValue, resourceUnavailable, commitFailed, undoFailed, authorizationError and notWritable. The maximum value of max-bindings is 2147483647.

The BulkPDU used by GetBulkRequest must be identical in structure to PDU, except that the error-status and error-index fields are replaced by non-repeaters and max-repetitions, both of type INTEGER (0..max-bindings). A VarBind pairs an ObjectName with a choice of a value, the unSpecified NULL used in retrieval requests, or one of three exception markers used in responses: noSuchObject, noSuchInstance and endOfMibView. A VarBindList is a SEQUENCE (SIZE (0..max-bindings)) OF VarBind.

SNMPv2 limits OBJECT IDENTIFIER values to a maximum of 128 sub-identifiers, where each sub-identifier has a maximum value of 2**32-1.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request carries a number to match the reply to it, a status saying whether it worked, and a list of names with values. The bulk request swaps the status for two counts that say how many rows to fetch.

sections.title: Reading a Table with GetNextRequest
sections.content:
On receipt of a GetNextRequest-PDU, the receiving entity processes each variable binding to produce a Response-PDU. For each binding, the variable is located which is in the lexicographically ordered list of the names of all variables accessible by this request and whose name is the first lexicographic successor of the requested name. The name and value of that located variable go into the response. If the requested name does not lexicographically precede the name of any variable accessible by the request, that is, there is no lexicographic successor, the binding in the response has its value field set to endOfMibView and its name field set to the requested name.

An important use of the GetNextRequest-PDU is the traversal of conceptual tables of information within a MIB. The semantics of the request, together with the method of identifying individual instances of objects in the MIB, provides access to related objects as if they enjoyed a tabular organization.

The RFC works through an example. The IP net-to-media Address Translation Table has three entries, with interface numbers, network addresses, physical addresses and types. The manager begins with a GetNextRequest naming sysUpTime, ipNetToMediaPhysAddress and ipNetToMediaType, and the agent answers with the current sysUpTime and the first entries of the two columns. The manager then repeats the request using the names it was just given, and each time the agent returns the next lexicographic name. When there are no further entries in the table, the agent responds with the variables that are next in the lexicographical ordering of the accessible object names, for example ipNetToMediaNetAddress and ipRoutingDiscards, and this response signals the end of the table to the manager.
sections.plainLanguage: To read a table, ask for the next name after the one you were given. Names are ordered, so the agent always knows which row comes next. When the names stop belonging to the table, you have reached the end.

sections.title: GetBulkRequest and Fewer Exchanges
sections.content:
The purpose of the GetBulkRequest-PDU is to request the transfer of a potentially large amount of data, including, but not limited to, the efficient and rapid retrieval of large tables. One of its aims is to minimize the number of protocol exchanges required to retrieve a large amount of management information.

Unlike the other request types, the successful processing of each variable binding generates zero or more variable bindings in the response, so the one-to-one mapping between request and response bindings does not apply. The values of the non-repeaters and max-repetitions fields specify what is wanted: one variable binding is requested for the first N variable bindings in the request, and M variable bindings are requested for each of the R remaining variable bindings. The total number of requested bindings is N plus M times R, where N is the minimum of the non-repeaters value and the number of bindings in the request, M is the value of the max-repetitions field, and R is the maximum of the number of bindings in the request minus N, and zero.

The response may be generated with fewer variable bindings than requested, for two reasons. If the message carrying the requested number of bindings would exceed a local constraint or the maximum message size of the request's source party, the response is generated with the ordered set of bindings with some at the end removed, so that the message is approximately equal to but no greater than that limit. The number removed has no relationship to N, M or R. The response may also be shorter if, for some iteration, all of the generated bindings have the value endOfMibView, in which case the bindings may be truncated after the relevant one.

The RFC demonstrates the same traversal of the IP net-to-media table with fewer exchanges, using a max-repetitions value of 2 and a non-repeaters value of 1. The first response returns sysUpTime and two entries of each of the two table columns, and the second response returns the last table row plus the variables that signal the end of the table.
sections.plainLanguage: The bulk request asks for many rows in one go. The first few names are asked for once each, and the rest are repeated a set number of times, which cuts the number of round trips needed to read a long table.

sections.title: Responses, Errors, Traps and Informs
sections.content:
A Response-PDU is generated only upon receipt of a GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, SetRequest or InformRequest. If the error-status field is non-zero, the value fields of the variable bindings are ignored. If both error-status and error-index are non-zero, the error-index is the index of the variable binding in the corresponding request for which the request failed, the first binding being index one. The value of the request-id field in a Response-PDU takes the value of the request-id in the request it answers, which lets an application match responses to outstanding requests and identify messages duplicated by the network.

A SetRequest is processed in two conceptual phases. In the first phase each variable binding is validated, and only if all validations succeed is the second phase entered, in which each variable is altered. The validations cover a variable that is not accessible (noAccess), one that does not exist and could never be created (noCreation), one that exists but cannot be modified (notWritable), a value of the wrong type, length or encoding, a value that could never be assigned (wrongValue), a name that does not exist but cannot be created under present circumstances (inconsistentName), a value that is presently inconsistent (inconsistentValue), and a resource that is presently unavailable (resourceUnavailable). If an assignment fails, all other assignments are undone and the error status becomes commitFailed; if it is not possible to undo all of them, the status becomes undoFailed. The RFC strongly encourages implementations to avoid both of those outcomes.

An SNMPv2-Trap-PDU is generated by an agent when an exceptional situation occurs. The destinations are found in the aclTable, and the variable-bindings field is built with sysUpTime.0 first, snmpTrapOID.0 second, then the variables named in the OBJECTS clause of the notification in order, and finally any additional variables the agent chooses to add. An InformRequest-PDU is generated by a manager that wishes to notify another manager of information in its own MIB view. The first two variable bindings are sysUpTime.0 and snmpEventID.i, and the receiver answers with a Response-PDU whose error status is noError.
sections.plainLanguage: A reply says either everything worked or gives a code and the position in the request where things went wrong. Setting values is checked first and only applied if every value passes, so a partly applied change is rolled back.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN SNMPv2 PDU TYPES AND THEIR TAGS

items.label: GetRequest
items.desc: Ask for the value of one or more named variables.

items.label: GetNextRequest
items.desc: Ask for the next variable in lexicographic order.

items.label: Response
items.desc: The answer to a request, with an error status if needed.

items.label: SetRequest
items.desc: Ask for the value of variables to be changed.

items.label: GetBulkRequest
items.desc: Ask for many variables at once, to read large tables quickly.

items.label: InformRequest
items.desc: One manager notifying another, and expecting an answer.

items.label: SNMPv2-Trap
items.desc: An unsolicited report of an exceptional situation, with no reply.

messages.label: RESPONSE
messages.note: Returns the next name in lexicographic order.

messages.label: GETNEXTREQUEST
messages.note: Repeats with the name just returned.

messages.label: RESPONSE WITH endOfMibView
messages.note: Signals that the table has been walked to its end.

viz.caption: THE ERROR STATUS CODES AND WHAT THEY MEAN

cells: The response would not fit in a message the sender could accept.
The request failed for a reason not covered by any other code.
The named variable is not accessible by this request.
The value has a type the variable does not take.
The value could under no circumstances be assigned to the variable.
The variable exists but cannot be modified.
An assignment failed and the other assignments were undone.
An assignment failed and the other assignments could not be undone.
